claims.text: Adding a small amount of lanthanum to a Zr-based metallic-glass alloy will enhance its glass-forming ability.
The baseline Zr-based alloy has moderate glass-forming ability.
The baseline Zr-based alloy tends to crystallize during cooling under conventional conditions.
Lanthanum addition increases atomic-size mismatch among the alloy constituents.
Lanthanum addition makes the alloy's mixing enthalpy more strongly negative.
Lanthanum atoms are significantly larger than Zr atoms and the other unspecified alloy constituents.
The size mismatch introduced by lanthanum creates structural distortion and disorder.
Lanthanum-induced chemical and structural disorder destabilizes potential crystalline nuclei.
Lanthanum-induced disorder raises the free-energy barrier for crystal nucleation during cooling.
The increased nucleation barrier favors formation of an amorphous phase.
Lanthanum addition will provide a greater critical-cooling-rate margin for glass formation.
Lanthanum addition will produce a larger glass-transition-related temperature window than the baseline alloy.
Lanthanum addition will suppress crystallization peaks relative to the baseline alloy.
The optimum lanthanum concentration depends on the overall Zr-based alloy composition and processing parameters.
Excessive lanthanum may cause phase separation.
Excessive lanthanum may promote unwanted intermetallic-compound formation.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome refers to an 'increased critical cooling rate margin,' whereas the falsification rule treats a decrease in the critical cooling rate as improvement. These may be reconcilable if 'margin' means processing tolerance, but the direction of the stated cooling-rate metric is ambiguous.
